kurals.tamil:
தீவினையார் அஞ்சார் விழுமியார் அஞ்சுவர்
தீவினை என்னும் செருக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Theevinaiyaar anjaar vizhumiyaar anjuvar,
Theevinai ennum serukku.
kurals.meaning: Those already steeped in wrongdoing feel no fear of the heady arrogance that evil deeds bring; only the truly noble are afraid of it.
kurals.elementary: Imagine two kids near a hot stove. One has touched it so many times he doesn’t even flinch anymore. The other is careful and keeps her hands away. This kural says good people are like the careful kid — they are scared of doing bad things, while people who do bad things all the time have stopped being scared at all.
kurals.university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a paradox: fear, usually a mark of weakness, is here the mark of excellence (விழுமியார், “the eminent”). The object of dread is not punishment but “the pride called evil-doing” (தீவினை என்னும் செருக்கு) — Parimelazhagar reads செருக்கு as the intoxication or swagger that evil deeds produce, which dulls conscience the more one indulges it. The couplet thus describes moral desensitization: habitual wrongdoers lose the very faculty of dread that protects the noble. This anticipates what Buddhist ethics calls hiri-ottappa (moral shame and moral dread) and Jewish ethics calls yirat cheit (fear of sin) — fear reconceived as a moral sense rather than cowardice.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O Janārdana, although these men, overtaken by greed, see no fault in killing one’s family or quarreling with friends, why should we, with knowledge of the sin, engage in these acts?”
hinduism.explanation: On the battlefield Arjuna contrasts the Kauravas, whose greed has blinded them to sin, with himself and his brothers, who can still see the wrongness of what they are about to do and recoil from it.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly Valluvar’s split: the wrongdoers feel no dread, while those with moral sight fear the sin.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong structural parallel (greed-blinded feel no fault vs. the discerning who dread sin); Krishna ultimately overrides Arjuna’s specific scruple, so the Gita’s larger arc differs.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The fear of the LORD is to hate evil: pride, and arrogancy, and the evil way, and the froward mouth, do I hate.”
christianity.explanation: Wisdom speaks in Proverbs, defining true reverence as a hatred of evil — and naming pride and arrogance first among the things hated.
christianity.tie_back: Links holy fear, the avoidance of evil, and the rejection of pride — the same triad as the Kural’s “dread of the pride of evil.”
christianity._accuracy_note: Close thematic fit; the biblical fear is directed toward God, whereas Valluvar’s dread is directed toward evil itself.

islam.quote_or_event: “Only those fear Allah, from among His servants, who have knowledge.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an ties genuine fear of God (khashyah) to knowledge: the more one truly understands, the more one is moved to reverent caution about wrongdoing.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes fear a sign of the elevated, not the base — those with understanding fear; the heedless do not.
islam._accuracy_note: Good parallel on fear as a mark of the wise; object is God rather than evil deeds as such.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Anyone whose fear of sin precedes his wisdom, his wisdom is enduring, but anyone whose wisdom precedes his fear of sin, his wisdom is not enduring.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa makes yirat cheit — fear of sin — the foundation on which lasting wisdom must stand.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts treat fear of wrongdoing as the defining trait of the truly excellent person.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close: explicit ‘fear of sin’ as the mark of the worthy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Monks, these two bright qualities guard the world. Which two? Conscience & concern.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names hiri (conscience/moral shame) and ottappa (concern/moral dread of the results of wrong action) as the ‘guardians of the world’ that hold society together.
buddhism.tie_back: Ottappa is almost a technical name for Valluvar’s theme: the dread of evil deeds that the noble keep and the corrupt have lost.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 2.9, Lokapala Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one conceptual match (moral dread as protective virtue).

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Hesiod’s account of the degenerate Iron Age, the goddesses Aidos (Shame) and Nemesis (Righteous Indignation) wrap themselves in white robes and abandon humankind for Olympus, leaving mortals with bitter sorrows and no defense against evil.
greek_mythology.explanation: For Hesiod, a healthy society depends on Aidos and Nemesis — an inner shame at wrongdoing and a dread of the retribution it provokes. When people stop feeling them, moral collapse follows.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Mirrors the Kural’s point that losing the dread of evil is itself the sign of the wicked; the noble keep Aidos.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good thematic parallel (shame/dread as moral guardians), framed mythically rather than as individual ethics.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “This sign, which is a kind of voice, first began to come to me when I was a child; it always forbids but never commands me to do anything which I am going to do.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates describes his daimonion, an inner warning that checks him before wrong or unwise action — an early philosophical image of conscience as a restraining dread.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s noble person is one whose inner alarm still sounds; Socrates is the classic example of such a person.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Conscience as inhibiting inner voice; Socrates’ sign is divine and idiosyncratic, not a general theory of moral fear.

kurals.tamil:
தீயவை தீய பயத்தலால் தீயவை
தீயினும் அஞ்சப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Theeyavai theeya payaththalaal theeyavai,
Theeyinum anjap padum.
kurals.meaning: Because evil deeds give rise to further evil, they should be feared even more than fire.
kurals.elementary: Fire can burn you, so you keep away from it. But a bad deed is even worse than fire — one bad deed leads to another bad deed, and then another, like sparks starting more fires. So we should be even more careful about doing bad things than about touching fire.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on a deliberate pun: தீ means both “evil” and “fire,” and தீயவை (“evil things”) sounds like “fiery things.” Valluvar’s argument is comparative — fire burns only what it touches and can be put out, but evil propagates, generating consequences for both the victim and the doer (Pulavar Kesigan: ‘to others and to oneself’). Evil is therefore self-replicating in a way fire only resembles. The same insight — that wrongdoing breeds more wrongdoing — appears in the rabbinic dictum that ‘one transgression leads to another’ and in Aeschylus’s image of the evil deed that begets its own offspring.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Thus the wise living entity’s pure consciousness becomes covered by his eternal enemy in the form of lust, which is never satisfied and which burns like fire.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names desire (kāma) as the root that drives people to sin, likening it to a fire that only grows the more it is fed.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts use fire as the image of evil’s self-feeding growth; the Kural goes further, saying evil is worse than fire.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shared fire imagery and self-perpetuation; Gita targets desire as root of sin rather than evil deeds themselves.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.”
christianity.explanation: James describes a chain of generation: desire gives birth to sin, and sin, fully grown, gives birth to death.
christianity.tie_back: Same logic as ‘evil yields evil’ — wrongdoing is fertile and its offspring are destructive.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on evil’s generative chain; no explicit comparison to fire.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, those who devour the property of orphans unjustly are only consuming into their bellies fire. And they will be burned in a Blaze.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes an evil deed as literally being fire in disguise: the unjust gain that seems like nourishment is burning the wrongdoer from within.
islam.tie_back: Like Valluvar, it equates evil with fire — and implies that evil is the more dangerous because it is not recognized as fire.
islam._accuracy_note: Evil-as-fire image; the verse concerns a specific sin (orphans’ property) rather than evil in general.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For one commandment leads to another commandment, and transgression leads to another transgression; For the reward for performing a commandment is another commandment and the reward for committing a transgression is a transgression.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Azzai observes that sin has momentum: each transgression makes the next one easier, so the ‘wage’ of sin is simply more sin.
judaism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s reasoning — evil is to be feared because it produces more evil.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on ‘evil begets evil’; lacks the fire comparison.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Truly, an evil deed committed does not immediately bear fruit, like milk that does not turn sour all at once. But smoldering, it follows the fool like fire covered by ashes.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares an unripened evil deed to embers hidden under ash — quiet for now, but still burning and certain to scorch the one who carries it.
buddhism.tie_back: Fire and evil are fused in one image, and the danger is precisely that evil keeps burning after the act.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Excellent: evil explicitly as hidden fire that keeps producing harm.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “It is the evil deed that afterwards begets more iniquity like its own breed; but when a house is righteous, the lot of its children is blessed always.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The chorus of Agamemnon reflects on the curse of the house of Atreus, in which each crime (Atreus’s feast, Iphigenia’s sacrifice) breeds the next murder.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The same principle as ‘evil yields evil’, dramatized across generations.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on the generative nature of evil deeds.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Gorgias, Socrates defends the startling thesis that doing injustice is the greatest of evils — worse even than suffering it — because it corrupts the soul of the doer.
philosophy.explanation: For Socrates, physical harms like burns or wounds damage only the body, while wrongdoing damages the soul, the most precious thing a person has.
philosophy.tie_back: Parallels the Kural’s ranking: evil is to be feared more than fire because its harm is deeper and self-inflicted.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong on ‘evil worse than physical harm’; less on evil’s self-multiplying character.

kurals.tamil:
அறிவினுள் எல்லாந் தலையென்ப தீய
செறுவார்க்கும் செய்யா விடல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Arivinul ellaan thalaiyenba theeya,
Seruvaarkkum seyyaa vidal.
kurals.meaning: The wise say that the highest of all wisdom is to refrain from doing evil even to those who harm us.
kurals.elementary: If someone knocks down your sandcastle, you might want to knock down theirs. But the smartest thing — smarter than anything in any book — is to not do something bad back. Being kind even to someone who was mean to you is the cleverest thing of all.
kurals.university: Here Valluvar relocates the virtue of non-retaliation from the realm of emotion (forgiveness) into the realm of intellect: it is the ‘head’ (தலை) of all knowledge. செறுவார் means those who actively hurt or oppress one — genuine enemies, not mere irritants. The claim is that true intelligence sees what the vengeful cannot: that returning evil only multiplies it (the logic of 202) and binds the retaliator to the same consequences. The idea stands in striking agreement with Socrates in the Crito, who argues on rational grounds that one must never return wrong for wrong.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not envious but is a kind friend to all living entities, who does not think himself a proprietor and is free from false ego, who is equal in both happiness and distress, who is tolerant, always satisfied, self-controlled… such a devotee of Mine is very dear to Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the ideal devotee as without hatred toward any being (adveṣṭā sarva-bhūtānām) and tolerant (kṣamī) — a person who does not return hostility.
hinduism.tie_back: Shares the ideal of non-hostility toward all, including those who harm; less explicit about enemies than the Kural.
hinduism._accuracy_note: General non-hatred and forbearance; not specifically about refraining from retaliation against aggressors.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Recompense to no man evil for evil… Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.”
christianity.explanation: Paul instructs believers never to repay wrong with wrong, but to defeat evil by doing good.
christianity.tie_back: A direct parallel: do no evil even to those who have done evil to you.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one; Paul frames it as moral duty, Valluvar as supreme wisdom.

islam.quote_or_event: “And not equal are the good deed and the bad. Repel [evil] by that [deed] which is better; and thereupon the one whom between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he was a devoted friend.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches responding to hostility with something better than the offense, promising that enmity can turn into friendship.
islam.tie_back: Same refusal to answer harm with harm, plus a practical wisdom about its effects.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong parallel; adds a positive response (goodness) beyond mere abstention.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah forbids taking revenge or even nursing a grudge, grounding the command in love of neighbour.
judaism.tie_back: Forbids retaliation, the core of the Kural; Torah’s scope is framed around one’s own people.
judaism._accuracy_note: Clear prohibition of revenge; narrower stated scope than Valluvar’s ‘enemies’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is a law eternal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha presents non-retaliation as a law of nature: returning hatred only perpetuates it; only non-hatred ends it.
buddhism.tie_back: Like Valluvar, frames non-retaliation as insight into how things work — the highest wisdom.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one, framed as eternal law (wisdom) rather than mere command.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the close of the Oresteia, Athena persuades the Furies to abandon the endless blood-for-blood vendetta of the house of Atreus and accept a court of justice, transforming them into the ‘Kindly Ones’.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek myth mostly celebrates vengeance; the Eumenides is its famous turning point, where wisdom (Athena) breaks the cycle of retaliation.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Next-best match: wisdom ending retaliation, though via public justice rather than personal non-retaliation.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weak-moderate; replaces private vengeance with law rather than teaching personal forbearance.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Then we ought not to retaliate or render evil for evil to any one, whatever evil we may have suffered from him.”
philosophy.explanation: In prison, Socrates reasons with Crito that since doing wrong is never right, returning wrong for wrong can never be right either.
philosophy.tie_back: Exact parallel, reached — as in the Kural — through reason rather than sentiment.

kurals.tamil:
மறந்தும் பிறன்கேடு சூழற்க சூழின்
அறஞ்சூழும் சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு.
kurals.transliteration:
Marandhum pirankedu soozharka soozhin,
Aransoozhum soozhndhavan kedu.
kurals.meaning: Do not plot another’s ruin even absent-mindedly; if you do, Virtue itself will plot the ruin of the one who plotted.
kurals.elementary: It’s like throwing a boomerang at someone — it comes flying back at you. This kural says even thinking up a plan to hurt someone is like that boomerang: goodness itself will turn the plan around so it lands on you.
kurals.university: The verb சூழ் (‘to plan, surround, encompass’) is repeated three times, mirroring the plot and counter-plot: the schemer ‘surrounds’ another’s ruin, and Aram (Virtue, personified by Solomon Pappaiah as அறக்கடவுள், the deity of Virtue) ‘surrounds’ the schemer’s ruin in turn. Note the extreme standard set by மறந்தும் (‘even in forgetfulness’): not merely the deed but even a passing intention to harm is forbidden. The textual tradition is worth noting — Project Madurai and thirukkural.net print அறஞ்சூழம், but the standard reading followed by commentators and kuraltheni.com is அறஞ்சூழும் (‘will plot’). The ‘plot that recoils on the plotter’ is a near-universal motif, from Haman’s gallows to Hesiod’s ‘evil planned harms the plotter most’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata’s lac-house episode, Duryodhana sends his agent Purochana to build a flammable house at Varanavata and burn the Pandavas alive; forewarned by Vidura, the Pandavas escape through a tunnel, and Purochana perishes in the very fire prepared for them.
hinduism.explanation: The agent of the murderous plot is consumed by his own scheme, while the intended victims survive.
hinduism.tie_back: A narrative illustration of the Kural: the plot to ruin others encompasses the plotter.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Jatugriha Parva (Ganguli; paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of episode; Duryodhana himself is not ruined here (only his agent), and his downfall comes later.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein: and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb warns that schemes meant to trap others become traps for the schemer.
christianity.tie_back: Direct parallel to the plot rebounding on the plotter.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one; lacks the Kural’s ‘even in forgetfulness’ intensifier.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Due to] arrogance in the land and plotting of evil; but the evil plot does not encompass except its own people.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an states as a divine law that evil scheming closes in on those who devise it.
islam.tie_back: Even the verb matches: the Arabic yaḥīqu (‘encompasses’) corresponds to Valluvar’s சூழ் (‘surround, encompass’).

judaism.quote_or_event: “So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai.”
judaism.explanation: Haman plotted to destroy Mordecai and the Jews of Persia; his plan was reversed and he died on the gallows he had built for his enemy.
judaism.tie_back: The classic Jewish story of the plot recoiling on the plotter.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel; divine agency is implicit in Esther.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like fine dust thrown against the wind, evil falls back upon that fool who offends an inoffensive, pure and guiltless man.”
buddhism.explanation: Harm aimed at the innocent blows back into the face of the one who threw it.
buddhism.tie_back: Same boomerang structure as the Kural.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “He does mischief to himself who does mischief to another, and evil planned harms the plotter most.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns his brother Perses that unjust scheming damages the schemer above all.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Almost a translation of the Kural’s second line.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 265–266 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Essentially one-to-one, including emphasis on planning (not just doing).

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He who does wrong does wrong against himself. He who acts unjustly acts unjustly to himself, because he makes himself bad.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius argues that the primary victim of wrongdoing is the wrongdoer, whose character is degraded by the act.
philosophy.tie_back: Shares the conclusion that harm aimed at others lands on oneself, though via inner corruption rather than cosmic retribution.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Mechanism differs (self-corruption vs. Virtue’s counter-plot), conclusion same.

kurals.tamil:
இலன்என்று தீயவை செய்யற்க செய்யின்
இலனாகும் மற்றும் பெயர்த்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Ilan endru theeyavai seyyarka seyyin,
Ilanaagum matrum peyarththu.
kurals.meaning: Do not commit evil on the excuse that you are poor; if you do, you will only become poorer still.
kurals.elementary: Suppose you have no snacks and you take someone else’s lunch. Now nobody trusts you, nobody shares with you, and you might get in big trouble. You end up with even less than before! Being poor is never a good reason to do bad things — it just makes things worse.
kurals.university: Valluvar anticipates the most sympathetic excuse for wrongdoing — need — and refuses it. இலன் (‘one who has not’) is echoed in the second line (இலனாகும், ‘becomes one who has not’) with பெயர்த்து (‘again, once more’), producing a circular structure that mirrors the poverty trap itself: evil committed to escape want returns one to want. Most commentators (Mu. Varadarasan, Pappaiah, Kalaignar) read இலன் as ‘poor’; Pulavar Kesigan offers an alternative — ‘do not harm someone because he is without support’ — which shifts the focus to exploiting the weak. On the dominant reading, the couplet makes a hard-headed point: ill-gotten means destroy trust, reputation and future prosperity, and so perpetuate the very lack they were meant to cure.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Being bound by hundreds and thousands of desires, by lust and anger, they secure money by illegal means for sense gratification.”
hinduism.explanation: In describing the ‘demoniac’ nature, the Gita names acquiring wealth by unjust means as a mark of those who then sink into ever-lower states.
hinduism.tie_back: Condemns the unjust pursuit of wealth and links it to downfall; does not address poverty as an excuse.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Next-best: unjust acquisition leads to ruin; motive is greed rather than need.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.”
christianity.explanation: Paul redirects the thief — often driven by want — to honest labour, which not only meets need but produces surplus to give away.
christianity.tie_back: Rejects wrongdoing as a remedy for need; honest work, not theft, is the way out of lack.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the rejection of theft for need; lacks the ‘you’ll become poorer’ consequence.

islam.quote_or_event: “Satan threatens you with poverty and orders you to immorality, while Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an identifies the fear of poverty as a tool Satan uses to push people into wrongdoing, while God’s promise is abundance.
islam.tie_back: Exposes poverty-as-excuse for evil as a deception; the path of evil does not lead to plenty.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match on poverty-fear as a false motive for sin.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me: Lest I be full, and deny thee… or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain.”
judaism.explanation: Agur prays to be spared extreme poverty precisely because he knows it tempts a person to steal and so to dishonour God.
judaism.tie_back: Recognizes poverty’s pull toward wrongdoing — the very temptation the Kural forbids yielding to.
judaism._accuracy_note: Acknowledges the temptation; prays against it rather than stating its self-defeating result.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Cakkavatti Sihanada Sutta, a king neglects to give to the needy; poverty spreads, a poor man steals, and the king’s response sets off a cascade — theft, violence, lying — in which society grows ever poorer and human life-span declines.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha narrates a spiral in which poverty leads to theft, and theft leads to further degradation and deprivation.
buddhism.tie_back: Illustrates the Kural’s trap on a social scale: wrongdoing born of want produces more want.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; collective rather than individual, and places blame also on the ruler’s neglect.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Wealth should not be seized: god-given wealth is much better; for if a man take great wealth violently and perforce, or if he steal it through his tongue… the gods soon blot him out and make that man’s house low, and wealth attends him only for a little time.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns his brother that riches got by force or fraud are short-lived; the gods reduce such a man’s household.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Same economic moral: unjust gain ends in greater loss.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 320–326 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong on outcome; Hesiod addresses greed generally, not specifically poverty as excuse.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Gorgias, Polus cites Archelaus, who rose from a slave woman’s son to king of Macedon through murder and treachery, as proof that injustice pays. Socrates replies that Archelaus, far from being enviable, is the most wretched of men.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates rejects the idea that wrongdoing is a rational escape from low estate: the unjust man gains power but loses the true good of his soul.
philosophy.tie_back: Next-best: rejects the excuse of lowly circumstance for evil, and argues the wrongdoer ends up poorer in what matters.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the ‘poverty’ is of the soul rather than material.

kurals.tamil:
தீப்பால தான்பிறர்கண் செய்யற்க நோய்ப்பால
தன்னை அடல்வேண்டா தான்.
kurals.transliteration:
Theeppaala thaanpirarkan seyyarka noippaala,
Thannai adalvendaa thaan.
kurals.meaning: Whoever does not wish to be tormented by suffering should never do evil to others.
kurals.elementary: If you don’t want anyone to pull your hair, don’t pull anyone else’s hair. This kural says: if you don’t want bad things to happen to you, don’t do bad things to other people.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on a pair of parallel compounds — தீப்பால (‘things of the evil kind’) done to others, and நோய்ப்பால (‘things of the suffering kind’) that might afflict oneself — so that the grammar itself enacts reciprocity. Commentators agree the sense is causal: suffering that ‘attacks’ (அடல்) a person is the return of the evil he has done. The argument is prudential and universal — anyone who does not want pain has a reason not to inflict it — which makes this Valluvar’s version of the negative Golden Rule. That rule appears independently in the Mahabharata, in Hillel, in Isocrates, in the Buddha and in the Gospels, one of the most striking convergences in world ethics.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One should never do that to another which one regards as injurious to one’s own self. This, in brief, is the rule of Righteousness.”
hinduism.explanation: Brihaspati tells Yudhishthira that all dharma can be summed up in this one principle, adding that when one injures another, the injured turns and injures the injurer.
hinduism.tie_back: The negative Golden Rule plus the reciprocal consequence — both halves of the Kural.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus states the Golden Rule in positive form as the summary of the Law and the Prophets.
christianity.tie_back: Same reciprocity principle, phrased positively where the Kural is negative.
christianity._accuracy_note: Positive formulation; lacks the explicit self-protective consequence.

islam.quote_or_event: “None of you will have faith till he wishes for his (Muslim) brother what he likes for himself.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes wishing for others what one wishes for oneself a condition of true faith.
islam.tie_back: Reciprocity principle at the heart of both; the hadith is framed as faith, the Kural as consequence.
islam._accuracy_note: Golden Rule parallel; positive and faith-centered rather than consequence-centered.

judaism.quote_or_event: “That which is hateful to you do not do to another; that is the entire Torah, and the rest is its interpretation.”
judaism.explanation: Asked to teach the whole Torah on one foot, Hillel summarizes it as the negative Golden Rule.
judaism.tie_back: Same negative formulation as the Kural: don’t do to others what you don’t want to suffer.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one; Kural adds the explicit consequence of suffering.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “All tremble at violence; all fear death. Putting oneself in the place of another, one should not kill nor cause another to kill.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha grounds non-harming in empathy: since everyone fears pain as I do, I should not inflict it.
buddhism.tie_back: Same self-comparison logic underlying the Kural’s reciprocity.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Empathy-based rather than consequence-based, but the same self/other symmetry.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On his journey to Athens, Theseus defeats a series of brigands by giving each the fate he inflicted on travellers — Sciron is hurled off his own cliff, Procrustes is fitted to his own bed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Plutarch notes that Theseus punished the violent by the very violence they had used on others.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Dramatizes the reciprocity the Kural warns of: what you do to others comes back upon you.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates reciprocal retribution; not an ethical rule of restraint as in the Kural.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Do not do to others that which angers you when they do it to you.”
philosophy.explanation: Isocrates, writing in the voice of King Nicocles, gives his subjects this compact rule of conduct.
philosophy.tie_back: A classical Greek statement of the negative Golden Rule, nearly identical in form to the Kural.

kurals.tamil:
எனைப்பகை யுற்றாரும் உய்வர் வினைப்பகை
வீயாது பின்சென்று அடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Enaippakai yutraarum uyvar vinaippakai,
Veeyaadhu pinsendru adum.
kurals.meaning: People can survive any enmity, however great; but the enmity of their own evil deeds never dies — it follows them and destroys them.
kurals.elementary: You can hide from a bully, run away, or make friends again. But the bad things you did are like a shadow-monster that follows you everywhere. You can’t hide from it or run away from it, because it comes from you.
kurals.university: The contrast is between பகை (enmity) from others and வினைப்பகை (‘the enmity of deeds’) — Valluvar’s striking personification of karma as a relentless personal foe. Human enemies can be escaped, appeased or outlived (உய்வர், ‘they survive’); the enemy that is one’s own past action ‘does not perish’ (வீயாது), ‘goes behind’ (பின்சென்று) and ‘kills’ (அடும்). The image of pursuit is shared with the Greek Erinyes, who hound Orestes across the world, and with the Mahabharata’s calf that unfailingly finds its mother among a thousand cows. The couplet thus answers a common hope of wrongdoers — that they might outrun consequences.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As the young calf is able to recognise its dam from among a thousand cows, so does the previous acts of a man pursue him (in all his different transformations).”
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma teaches Yudhishthira that past deeds track down their doer as unerringly as a calf finds its mother.
hinduism.tie_back: Same image of deeds pursuing their doer without fail.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on pursuit; lacks the Kural’s contrast with human enemies.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if ye will not do so, behold, ye have sinned against the LORD: and be sure your sin will find you out.”
christianity.explanation: Moses warns the tribes that a broken commitment will not stay hidden: the sin itself will track them down.
christianity.tie_back: Sin as a pursuer that will find the sinner — the Kural’s ‘enmity of deeds’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close personification of sin as pursuer.

islam.quote_or_event: “Paradise is not [obtained] by your wishful thinking nor by that of the People of the Scripture. Whoever does a wrong will be recompensed for it, and he will not find besides Allah a protector or a helper.”
islam.explanation: No identity or wishful hope shields a wrongdoer from the consequences of his wrong.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, denies any escape from the recompense of one’s deeds.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on inescapability; lacks pursuit imagery.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Moreover he saw a skull floating on the face of the water. He said to it: because you drowned others, they drowned you. And in the end, they that drowned you will be drowned.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel reads a floating skull as proof that violent deeds pursue their doers through a chain of consequences.
judaism.tie_back: Deeds track down those who commit them, generation after generation.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on inescapable retribution for deeds.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Neither in the sky nor in mid-ocean, nor by entering into mountain clefts, nowhere in the world is there a place where one may escape from the results of evil deeds.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists every conceivable hiding place and declares none of them safe from the fruit of evil kamma.
buddhism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s claim: one may escape anything except one’s own evil deeds.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After killing his mother Clytemnestra, Orestes is hunted across Greece by the Erinyes (Furies), who track him by the scent of blood and will not relent until his case is judged at Athens.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Furies are the Greek personification of guilt’s relentless pursuit of a wrongdoer.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A living image of Valluvar’s ‘enmity of deeds’ that follows and destroys.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; excellent match on pursuit by one’s own deed.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The difficulty, my friends, is not in avoiding death, but in avoiding unrighteousness; for that runs faster than death.”
philosophy.explanation: Condemned, Socrates says death — the slower runner — has caught him, but unrighteousness — the faster — has overtaken his accusers.
philosophy.tie_back: Wrongdoing as a swift pursuer that overtakes its doers — close to the Kural’s image.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Pursuit metaphor for wrongdoing; Socrates contrasts it with death rather than with human enemies.

kurals.tamil:
தீயவை செய்தார் கெடுதல் நிழல்தன்னை
வீயாது அடிஉறைந் தற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Theeyavai seydhaar kedudhal nizhaldhannai,
Veeyaadhu adiyuraindh thatru.
kurals.meaning: Ruin clings to those who do evil just as a person’s shadow never leaves him but stays right at his feet.
kurals.elementary: Try running away from your shadow — you can’t! It sticks to your feet wherever you go. This kural says trouble sticks to people who do bad things in the same way. It follows them everywhere.
kurals.university: Valluvar sharpens the pursuit image of 207 into a simile of inseparability: the shadow does not merely follow but ‘dwells at the feet’ (அடியுறை) — the phrase also evokes a servant or dependent who lives at one’s feet. A shadow is produced by the person himself, so the image implies that ruin is not an external punishment but a by-product of one’s own action, as inseparable as it is self-generated. The text itself shows a scribal wrinkle: Project Madurai and thirukkural.net read ‘அஇஉறைந்’, an evident typographical corruption; ytamizh.com and kuruvirotti.com give அடிஉறைந் (‘dwelling at the feet’), the reading adopted here. The shadow simile famously also appears in the second verse of the Dhammapada, but applied to good deeds.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “According as one acts, according as one behaves, so does he become. The doer of good becomes good, the doer of evil becomes evil.”
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad teaches that deeds do not merely earn outcomes but reshape the very being of the doer.
hinduism.tie_back: Ruin is inseparable from the evil-doer because he becomes what he does — the inner logic behind Valluvar’s shadow.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Foundational karma statement; lacks the shadow image.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that consequences are bound to actions as a harvest is bound to its seed.
christianity.tie_back: Like the shadow, the harvest is produced by the doer himself and cannot be separated from him.
christianity._accuracy_note: Different image (sowing) for the same inseparability of act and consequence.

islam.quote_or_event: “And [for] every person We have imposed his fate upon his neck, and We will produce for him on the Day of Resurrection a record which he will encounter spread open.”
islam.explanation: Each person’s deeds and their outcomes are fastened to him like a collar at the neck — impossible to shake off.
islam.tie_back: Close to the shadow image: consequences are attached to the person’s own body.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He who performs one commandment acquires for himself one advocate, and he who commits one transgression acquires for himself one accuser.”
judaism.explanation: Each sin creates a lasting ‘accuser’ that stays with the sinner until judgment.
judaism.tie_back: Each evil act generates a constant companion of ill — a moral shadow.
judaism._accuracy_note: Accuser-companion metaphor; judicial rather than shadow imagery.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If with an impure mind a person speaks or acts suffering follows him like the wheel that follows the foot of the ox.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada opens with a pair of verses: suffering follows evil like the cart-wheel follows the ox, and (verse 2) happiness follows good like a never-departing shadow.
buddhism.tie_back: The same simile family — inseparable following at the feet — used for exactly the same point.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one; the shadow image itself appears in the paired verse 2 for good deeds.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the opening of the Odyssey, Zeus complains that mortals blame the gods for their misfortunes, when in truth their sorrows beyond fate come from their own reckless folly — citing Aegisthus, who was warned yet did evil and was destroyed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s Zeus insists that much human ruin is self-generated, flowing from one’s own wrongdoing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the shadow, ruin is produced by the person himself, not imposed from outside.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; shares self-caused ruin, not the image of constant accompaniment.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Myth of Er, souls are shown receiving, for every wrong they did in life, a penalty ten times over, before choosing their next lives — carrying their characters with them.
philosophy.explanation: Plato portrays the consequences of injustice as following the soul even beyond death.
philosophy.tie_back: Next-best: consequences cannot be shed, even at death.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; afterlife framework rather than shadow-like present accompaniment.

kurals.tamil:
தன்னைத்தான் காதல னாயின் எனைத்தொன்றும்
துன்னற்க தீவினைப் பால்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thannaiththaan kaadhala naayin enaiththondrum,
Thunnarka theevinaip paal.
kurals.meaning: If a person truly loves himself, let him not go near evil of any kind, however small.
kurals.elementary: If you love yourself, you take care of yourself — you brush your teeth and wear a helmet on your bike. This kural says that taking care of yourself also means staying away from bad deeds, even tiny ones, because they end up hurting you.
kurals.university: Valluvar here turns self-love (தன்னைத்தான் காதலன்) — often treated as a vice — into the very motive for virtue: anyone who genuinely wishes himself well will keep away from evil. The key intensifier is எனைத்தொன்றும் (‘any whatsoever, however slight’), and the verb துன்னற்க means ‘do not approach or come near’, implying avoidance of the whole territory of evil (தீவினைப் பால், ‘the side/portion of evil’) rather than only its grave acts. This is a form of ‘enlightened self-interest’: properly understood, self-love and morality coincide. Aristotle makes the same argument in Nicomachean Ethics IX.8, and the Dhammapada puts it in almost the same words: ‘If one holds oneself dear, one should diligently watch oneself.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One must deliver himself with the help of his mind, and not degrade himself. The mind is the friend of the conditioned soul, and his enemy as well.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that a person can be his own friend or his own enemy; true self-friendship means raising oneself rather than sinking into what degrades.
hinduism.tie_back: Same idea that genuine self-regard requires restraining oneself from what harms.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Self-as-friend theme; not specific about small evils.

christianity.explanation: Paul urges believers to keep away from every form of evil, not only its gross expressions.
christianity.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s ‘however small’ and ‘do not go near’ — avoiding the whole range of evil.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches scope of avoidance; lacks the self-love motive.

islam.quote_or_event: “So whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it, And whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it.”
islam.explanation: Nothing is too small to count: even an atom’s weight of evil will be shown to its doer.
islam.tie_back: Supports the Kural’s warning against evil ‘however small’ — every speck returns to oneself.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on smallness; motive is accountability rather than self-love.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And be careful with a light commandment as with a grave one… reckon… the gain [that may be obtained through the committing] of a transgression against the loss [entailed] thereby.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Judah the Prince advises weighing any apparent gain from a sin against the loss it brings, and treating light matters as seriously as grave ones.
judaism.tie_back: Same prudential self-interest and refusal to treat any wrong as trivial.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on cost-benefit self-interest and smallness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If one holds oneself dear, one should diligently watch oneself.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that genuine self-love expresses itself as vigilant self-guarding against wrong.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost a verbatim counterpart of ‘if one loves oneself’ in the Kural.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on self-love as motive for vigilance; see also Dhp 121 on small evils.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Prodicus’s fable, the young Heracles at a crossroads is approached by Vice, who offers an easy road of pleasure, and Virtue, who offers a steep road; he chooses Virtue as the path that truly benefits him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Heracles’ choice treats virtue as what is genuinely good for oneself, and vice as a flattering path to self-harm.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Next-best: choosing virtue out of true regard for one’s own good.
greek_mythology.source: Prodicus, ‘The Choice of Heracles’ in Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21–34 (paraphrase)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; about choosing a life-path, not avoiding small evils.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Therefore the good man should be a lover of self (for he will both himself profit by doing noble acts, and will benefit his fellows), but the wicked man should not; for he will hurt both himself and his neighbours, following as he does evil passions.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle distinguishes true self-love, which seeks the noble, from the vulgar kind that grasps at pleasures and harms the self.
philosophy.tie_back: Same insight: rightly understood, loving oneself means keeping away from evil.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.8, 1169a (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on self-love grounding virtue.

kurals.tamil:
அருங்கேடன் என்பது அறிக மருங்கோடித்
தீவினை செய்யான் எனின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Arungedan enbadhu arika marungodith,
Theevinai seyyaan enin.
kurals.meaning: Know that a person who never strays from the right path to do evil is safe from ruin.
kurals.elementary: When you walk on a narrow bridge, you’re safe as long as you don’t step off the sides. This kural says life is like that bridge: if you never wander off the good path to do bad things, nothing can really ruin you.
kurals.university: The chapter closes on a note of assurance rather than warning. அருங்கேடன் combines அரு (‘rare/absent’) with கேடு (‘ruin’): ‘one for whom ruin is rare or impossible’. The pivotal image is மருங்கோடி — ‘running off to the side’ — which pictures righteousness as a straight road and evil as a swerve off it; Parimelazhagar and later commentators read it as ‘deviating from the proper path’. After nine couplets on the consequences of evil, Valluvar states the positive corollary: since ruin comes from one’s own deeds, the one who does not swerve has nothing to fear. The swerve metaphor has close parallels in Proverbs (‘turn not to the right hand nor to the left’), in the Isha Upanishad’s prayer against ‘crooked’ sin, and in Aristotle’s virtue as a mean between deviations.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O god Agni, knowing all things that are manifested, lead us by the good path to the felicity; remove from us the devious attraction of sin.”
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad’s closing prayer asks the divine to keep us on the good path (supathā) and away from ‘crooked’ (juhurāṇam) sin.
hinduism.tie_back: Same picture of a straight good path and evil as a crooked deviation from it.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong path/deviation imagery; framed as prayer rather than assurance.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Turn not to the right hand nor to the left: remove thy foot from evil.”
christianity.explanation: The father in Proverbs urges his son to keep a straight path, since swerving to either side leads into evil.
christianity.tie_back: Nearly identical to மருங்கோடி — evil as a sideways deviation from the straight road.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on the swerve image; the safety promise is implicit (4:26).

islam.quote_or_event: “And, [moreover], this is My path, which is straight, so follow it; and do not follow [other] ways, for you will be separated from His way.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an presents righteousness as one straight path and wrongdoing as side-roads that lead away from it.
islam.tie_back: Same straight-path imagery; not straying is the key to safety.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong path parallel; the promise is guidance rather than freedom from ruin.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ye shall observe to do therefore as the LORD your God hath commanded you: ye shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left.”
judaism.explanation: Moses commands Israel to keep exactly to the way of the commandments without deviation, followed by the promise that it may go well with them.
judaism.tie_back: Non-deviation leading to well-being — the Kural’s formula.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close; the verse after (5:33) gives the promise of well-being.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If on the hand there is no wound, one may carry even poison in it. Poison does not affect one who is free from wounds. For him who does no evil, there is no ill.”
buddhism.explanation: Just as poison cannot enter unbroken skin, harm finds no entry into the life of one who commits no evil.
buddhism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s assurance: the one who does no evil is safe from ruin.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Essentially one-to-one on ‘no evil, no ill’.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Daedalus warns his son Icarus to fly a middle course between sea and sun; Icarus, exhilarated, swerves upward toward the sun, the wax of his wings melts, and he falls into the sea.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth makes safety depend on keeping to the prescribed course, and ruin the result of veering off it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A vivid picture of மருங்கோடி — ruin comes from swerving from the right path.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; deviation is recklessness rather than moral evil.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Virtue, then, is a state of character concerned with choice, lying in a mean, i.e. the mean relative to us, this being determined by a rational principle.”
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, virtue is a middle course, and vices are deviations to one side (excess) or the other (deficiency).
philosophy.tie_back: Shares the geometry of the Kural: goodness as a line, evil as a veering off it.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.6, 1106b–1107a (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Structural parallel only; Aristotle does not promise freedom from misfortune.
